patient.name: Gary Whitfield
patient.complaint: Sudden severe upper abdominal pain, now spreading across the whole abdomen, for 6 hours
background: Knee osteoarthritis: buys ibuprofen over the counter, takes it most days
Months of burning epigastric pain at night, eased by food
Lives alone in Lewisham, drives a bus

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with sudden severe pain, a still patient and a rigid abdomen; the history (NSAIDs, diverticular disease, cirrhosis with ascites) tells you the cause.

points: Gary, 61, felt a **sudden stabbing epigastric pain** at 4 am.
Within hours the pain spread **across his whole abdomen**.
He lies **completely still**; coughing makes him wince.
He has vomited twice and feels hot.

steps.lead: Daily **ibuprofen** plus nocturnal epigastric pain points to a **peptic ulcer** that has now **perforated** into the peritoneal cavity.

visual.title: Where Gary's pain is now
visual.caption: It began in the epigastrium and is now **generalised**: the whole peritoneum is inflamed.

points: Abdomen: **rigid, board-like**, barely moves with breathing.

steps.lead: Gary has the full picture: guarding, rebound, rigidity, tachycardia and fever. His BP is holding for now; **hypotension** would mean he is getting worse.

steps.q: Why does Gary lie so still, while a patient with renal colic writhes?
o: Any movement stretches the inflamed peritoneum
His pain is visceral and poorly localised
steps.r: Peritonitis hurts with **every movement** of the inflamed parietal peritoneum, so patients lie still. Colic patients cannot get comfortable and roll around.

steps.lead: If Gary were too unwell to stand, a supine AXR could show **Rigler's sign**: gas on **both sides** of the bowel wall.

steps.title: Spot the cause from the history
head: Clue in the stem
Likely cause
rows: NSAIDs, steroids, ulcer pain, sudden epigastric onset
Days of RIF pain, then suddenly worse everywhere
Older, LIF pain, fever, known diverticula
AF, pain out of proportion, high lactate
Vomiting, distension, no flatus, then rigid
Cirrhosis with ascites, fever, little tenderness

steps.lead: Gary has no liver disease or ascites. In a cirrhotic patient, the same word, peritonitis, means a **different disease** with no perforation.

steps.text: SBP can look mild: fever, confusion or worsening ascites with only **mild tenderness**. Any cirrhotic with ascites who becomes unwell needs a **diagnostic tap**.
Exam rule: **sudden** severe pain + patient lying **still** + **rigid** abdomen = peritonitis until proven otherwise. Then name the cause from the history.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?' (erect chest X-ray for suspected perforation) or the test that finds the cause (CT abdomen and pelvis); for SBP, the ascitic neutrophil count.

points: ABCDE: airway patent, oxygen started, two large-bore cannulas.
Bloods sent: FBC, U&E, LFTs, CRP, amylase, lactate, group and save.

steps.title: Gary's admission bloods
steps.text: Raised inflammatory markers and lactate. Amylase is only mildly raised: **less than 3 times** normal points away from pancreatitis.

steps.q: Perforation is suspected. Which imaging comes first?
steps.r: **Erect chest X-ray** is the initial investigation, looking for free air under the diaphragm. Endoscopy is avoided when perforation is suspected.

steps.lead: Gary had ABCDE, bloods and surgical review, then an **erect chest X-ray** sitting upright for at least 10 minutes.

visual.title: Gary's erect chest X-ray
visual.caption: Crescents of gas under both hemidiaphragms: **pneumoperitoneum**, so a hollow viscus has perforated.

steps.lead: Peritonitis itself is a **clinical** diagnosis. Gary's **CT** shows the culprit: a perforated anterior duodenal ulcer with free fluid.

steps.title: Suspected peritonitis: investigation order
nodes: ABCDE, bloods, lactate, group and save
Erect CXR: free air under diaphragm?
steps.caption: Imaging should never delay resuscitation of a shocked patient.

visual.title: Ascitic fluid neutrophils (if SBP suspected)
visual.label: Example cirrhotic patient 480
visual.caption: **>250 neutrophils/µl** confirms SBP; culture most often grows **E. coli**.

steps.text: A normal erect CXR does **not** exclude perforation. If the clinical picture fits, go on to **CT**.
A supine AXR in a perforation can show **Rigler's sign** (both sides of the bowel wall outlined by gas).

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?' (NBM, IV fluids, oxygen, IV broad-spectrum antibiotics, urgent surgical review) and the definitive step (source control). For SBP, ciprofloxacin prophylaxis afterwards.

points: An hour later Gary is clammy and confused.
Urine output only **15 ml/h** through his catheter.

steps.lead: Gary now has **septic shock** from peritonitis: hypotension, low urine output and a rising lactate. Resuscitate now, alongside the surgical plan.

steps.q: What comes first for Gary now?
o: IV fluid bolus and IV broad-spectrum antibiotics
steps.r: Resuscitate first: **IV fluids and IV antibiotics** within the hour. Imaging and theatre follow; oral antibiotics are useless in shock.

steps.lead: Gary is **nil by mouth**, gets **oxygen**, **IV fluids**, **IV antibiotics**, **analgesia** and an **NG tube** to decompress his stomach.

steps.title: Gary's management
nodes: NBM, IV fluids, catheter, fluid balance
Blood cultures, then IV broad-spectrum antibiotics
steps.caption: Resuscitation and antibiotics run alongside getting the patient to theatre.

steps.lead: Gary goes to theatre for **laparoscopic repair** of the perforation with an omental patch and peritoneal washout.

visual.title: Gary's response to resuscitation and surgery
visual.caption: Falling lactate and rising urine output show that resuscitation and **source control** are working.

steps.lead: Gary needs no prophylaxis, but a cirrhotic patient after an **SBP** episode stays on **ciprofloxacin** to prevent another.

steps.text: Do **not** send suspected perforation for endoscopy: insufflated air can enlarge the hole. Antibiotics alone do not fix a leaking viscus; it needs **source control**.
After a perforated ulcer: PPI, test for **H. pylori** and eradicate if positive, and **stop the NSAID**.

science.exam: Science questions ask why a sign occurs (rebound tenderness, guarding, a still patient) or how SBP happens without a perforation (bacterial translocation).

steps.title: From ulcer to shock
nodes: Ulcer erodes through the duodenal wall
Acid, bile and bacteria spill into the peritoneum
Fluid leaks into the peritoneal cavity (third-spacing)
Systemic inflammatory response and septic shock
steps.caption: That is why Gary went from pain to hypotension within hours.

steps.lead: Gary's perforation released **gastric acid** (chemical irritation) and then bacteria (contamination) into his peritoneal cavity.
Gary's contamination was **not contained**, so the inflammation became **generalised**; third-spacing explains his falling BP.

steps.q: Why did Gary's blood pressure fall?
o: Fluid shifts into the inflamed peritoneum plus sepsis vasodilation
steps.r: Inflamed peritoneum leaks litres of fluid (**third-spacing**) and the systemic inflammatory response vasodilates. His Hb was normal, so this is not bleeding.

steps.lead: Gary's rigid abdomen is **guarding** (muscle reflex); the pain when the examiner let go was **rebound** from parietal irritation.
SBP happens in **ascites** without any hole: gut bacteria cross the bowel wall or arrive in the blood, which is why **E. coli** is typical.

steps.text: Localised to generalised: an inflamed appendix or diverticulum is often walled off by omentum. If it **perforates freely**, the whole peritoneum becomes involved.

mcq.q: What is Rigler's sign on abdominal X-ray?
o: A dilated loop shaped like a coffee bean
Gas on both sides of the bowel wall
mcq.r: Rigler's sign is air on **both** the luminal and peritoneal sides of the bowel wall: **perforation**.

mcq.q: Which is a late, severe sign of peritonitis?
mcq.r: **Hypotension** is a late/severe sign and suggests septic shock.

mcq.q: Which ascitic fluid neutrophil count confirms spontaneous bacterial peritonitis?
mcq.r: SBP is confirmed by **>250 neutrophils/µl** in ascitic fluid.

mcq.q: Which organism is most often grown in SBP?
mcq.r: **E. coli** is the most common organism on ascitic fluid culture.

mcq.q: Which is the initial investigation when perforation is suspected?
mcq.r: **Erect CXR** looks for free air under the diaphragm.

mcq.q: What is the gold standard for peritonitis?
o: Clinical diagnosis plus CT to find the cause
mcq.r: Diagnosis is **clinical**; **CT** identifies the underlying cause.

mcq.q: Which is part of immediate management of peritonitis?
o: Nil by mouth and IV broad-spectrum antibiotics
mcq.r: **NBM, IV fluids, oxygen and IV broad-spectrum antibiotics**, plus analgesia and NG tube if needed.

mcq.q: Which antibiotic is used for prophylaxis after an SBP episode?

o: Irritation of the parietal peritoneum on release of pressure
Reflex contraction of the abdominal wall
mcq.r: Rebound = **parietal peritoneal irritation** on release; guarding is the reflex muscle contraction.

mcq.q: How does SBP arise without a perforation?
o: Bacterial translocation across the gut wall
mcq.r: **Bacterial translocation** (or haematogenous spread) in a patient with ascites.

prompts.q: What is peritonitis and what are its common causes?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the stem gives you the cause through the history.

points.why: From viscus perforation or intra-abdominal infection.
NSAIDs or steroids in the history are the clue.
Localised RIF peritonitis that can become generalised.

points.p: Bowel ischaemia or perforated bowel obstruction
points.why: Both end in a perforated, contaminated abdomen.

prompts.q: How does peritonitis present on history and examination?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: a patient lying still with a rigid abdomen.

points.p: Severe abdominal pain worse on movement or coughing
Hypotension is a late, severe sign

prompts.q: What is Rigler's sign and what does it mean?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: AXR sign, different from free air on an erect CXR.

points.p: Gas visible on both sides of the bowel wall

points.why: E.g. perforated duodenal ulcer, or after surgery/instrumentation.

prompts.q: How is spontaneous bacterial peritonitis diagnosed, and what organism causes it?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: cirrhosis + ascites + unwell = tap the ascites.

points.why: Do it in any unwell cirrhotic with ascites.
A gut Gram-negative, consistent with translocation.

points.p: Occurs with ascites, usually cirrhosis, without perforation

prompts.q: Which features suggest peritonitis is progressing to septic shock?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: these lead-ins move you to resuscitation.

prompts.q: What is the first-line investigation for suspected perforation, and what does it show?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: erect CXR first, CT for the cause.

points.p: ABCDE, urgent surgical review and bloods first
points.why: Resuscitation does not wait for imaging.

points.p: CT abdomen/pelvis to find the cause
points.why: Gold standard: clinical diagnosis plus CT.

prompts.q: What is the immediate management of peritonitis?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: list the resuscitation bundle, then source control.

points.p: Analgesia and NG tube if needed

prompts.q: What is the definitive treatment of peritonitis, and what follows an SBP episode?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: fix the source; SBP is medical.

points.p: Treat the underlying cause: source control

points.p: Surgery, drainage or repair of the perforation
points.why: E.g. omental patch for a duodenal ulcer.

prompts.q: Why do guarding, rebound tenderness and a still patient occur in peritonitis?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: parietal peritoneum has somatic nerves.

points.p: Guarding: reflex contraction of abdominal wall muscles
Rebound: parietal peritoneal irritation on release of pressure
points.why: The peritoneum moves back and hurts.

points.p: Movement or coughing stretches the inflamed peritoneum

prompts.q: Why does perforation cause peritonitis, and why can it become generalised and cause shock?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: chemical, then bacterial; third-spacing.

points.why: GI contents released by hollow viscus perforation.

points.p: Localised peritonitis can generalise if not contained

glossary.Peritonitis: Inflammation of the peritoneum, the membrane lining the abdominal cavity and covering the organs.
glossary.Parietal peritoneum: The peritoneal layer lining the abdominal wall; it has somatic nerves, so pain is sharp and well localised.
glossary.Visceral peritoneum: The peritoneal layer covering the organs; autonomic nerves make its pain dull and poorly localised.
glossary.Guarding: Reflex tensing of the abdominal wall muscles when the inflamed area is pressed.
glossary.Rebound tenderness: Pain felt when pressure on the abdomen is suddenly released, from parietal peritoneal irritation.
glossary.Rigidity: Constant, involuntary board-like tension of the abdominal wall, typical of generalised peritonitis.
glossary.Board-like: Describes a rigid abdomen that feels hard like a board, classic of a perforated viscus.
glossary.Rigler's sign: Gas outlining both sides of the bowel wall on abdominal X-ray, indicating perforation.
glossary.Pneumoperitoneum: Free gas in the peritoneal cavity, usually from a perforated hollow organ.
glossary.Viscus: A hollow internal organ such as the stomach, duodenum or colon.
glossary.Perforation: A hole through the full thickness of the wall of a hollow organ.
glossary.SBP: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis: infection of ascitic fluid without a perforation, usually in cirrhosis.
glossary.Ascites: Fluid collecting in the peritoneal cavity, most often caused by cirrhosis.
glossary.Paracentesis: Inserting a needle into the abdomen to sample or drain ascitic fluid.
glossary.Ascitic tap: Diagnostic paracentesis: a small sample of ascitic fluid sent for cell count and culture.
glossary.Cirrhosis: End-stage scarring of the liver that causes portal hypertension and ascites.
glossary.Bacterial translocation: Gut bacteria crossing the bowel wall into lymph, blood or ascitic fluid.
glossary.Third-spacing: Fluid shifting out of the blood into tissues or body cavities, causing hypovolaemia.
glossary.Septic shock: Sepsis with hypotension needing vasopressors and a raised lactate despite fluid resuscitation.
glossary.Lactate: A product of anaerobic metabolism; a raised level signals tissue hypoperfusion.
glossary.NBM: Nil by mouth: nothing to eat or drink, usually before surgery.
glossary.NG tube: Nasogastric tube passed through the nose into the stomach to decompress it.
glossary.Erect chest X-ray: Chest film taken with the patient upright so free gas rises under the diaphragm.
glossary.Source control: Removing the cause of infection, for example repairing a perforation or draining an abscess.
glossary.Omental patch: Surgical repair of a perforated ulcer by plugging the hole with a piece of omentum.
glossary.Omentum: A fatty apron of peritoneum that can wall off local inflammation.
glossary.Laparotomy: Open surgery through a large incision in the abdominal wall.
glossary.Ciprofloxacin: A fluoroquinolone antibiotic used as prophylaxis after spontaneous bacterial peritonitis.
glossary.E. coli: Escherichia coli, a Gram-negative gut bacterium and the commonest cause of SBP.
glossary.Peptic ulcer: A break in the stomach or duodenal lining, often from NSAIDs or H. pylori.
glossary.NSAIDs: Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs such as ibuprofen; they raise peptic ulcer risk.
glossary.H. pylori: Helicobacter pylori, a stomach bacterium that causes peptic ulcers.
glossary.Diverticulitis: Inflammation of colonic diverticula, usually in the sigmoid colon, causing LIF pain.
glossary.ABCDE: Structured approach to an acutely unwell patient: airway, breathing, circulation, disability, exposure.
glossary.Amylase: Pancreatic enzyme; more than 3 times normal suggests pancreatitis, a mild rise occurs in perforation.

technique.stem: A 24 year old man has a 3 day history of abdominal pain that started around his umbilicus and moved to the right iliac fossa. This morning the pain suddenly spread across his whole abdomen. He is lying very still. His temperature is 38.6°C, pulse rate 124 bpm and BP 108/70 mmHg. There is guarding and rebound tenderness in all four quadrants.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Generalised peritonitis from a perforated appendix

steps.x: A diagnosis question: decide localised or generalised, then the cause.

clues: started around his umbilicus and moved to the right iliac fossa
suddenly spread across his whole abdomen
guarding and rebound tenderness in all four quadrants
steps.x: Classic appendicitis history, then a sudden spread: perforation. Lying still and signs in **all four quadrants** mean **generalised** peritonitis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Appendicitis that has perforated: **generalised peritonitis**.

elim: Gastroenteritis gives diarrhoea and a soft abdomen, not rebound everywhere.
Mesenteric adenitis follows a viral illness and lacks peritonism.
Renal colic patients writhe; no peritonism.
Uncomplicated appendicitis stays in the RIF; signs in all quadrants mean perforation.

steps.x: **B.** Rule: localised peritonitis (e.g. appendicitis) becomes **generalised** when it is not contained.

technique.stem: A 70 year old woman has a 1 day history of severe generalised abdominal pain. She takes naproxen for arthritis. Her pulse rate is 110 bpm and BP 118/74 mmHg. Her abdomen is rigid with guarding. An erect chest X-ray shows no free air under the diaphragm.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
o: Repeat erect chest X-ray in 24 hours

steps.x: It asks for the next investigation after a normal erect CXR.

clues: no free air under the diaphragm
steps.x: NSAID use plus peritonism: perforation is still likely. A normal erect CXR does **not** exclude it.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **CT abdomen and pelvis** confirms perforation and identifies the cause.

elim: Ultrasound is poor for free gas and the cause of peritonitis.
Waiting 24 hours delays surgery in a peritonitic patient.
Amylase helps for pancreatitis but will not show a perforation.
Endoscopy is avoided when perforation is suspected.

steps.x: **B.** Rule: clinical diagnosis plus **CT** to find the cause.

technique.stem: A 66 year old man with diverticular disease has generalised abdominal pain and a rigid abdomen. His temperature is 38.9°C, pulse rate 132 bpm, BP 82/48 mmHg and respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute. His urine output is 10 ml/hour.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: IV fluid resuscitation and IV broad-spectrum antibiotics
Oral co-amoxiclav and review in 24 hours

steps.x: Initial management of an unstable patient.
Peritonitis with hypotension, fever and oliguria: **septic shock**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Urgent resuscitation: **IV fluids and IV antibiotics**, then surgical source control.

elim: Imaging must not delay resuscitation in shock.
Oral antibiotics are inadequate in septic shock.
A PPI does not treat septic shock or a colonic source.
Colonoscopy risks enlarging a perforation.

steps.x: **B.** Rule: hypotension + low urine output + high lactate = resuscitate now.

technique.stem: A 55 year old man with alcohol-related cirrhosis and ascites has a fever and mild abdominal discomfort. Ascitic fluid has a neutrophil count of 520 cells/µl and grows Escherichia coli. CT shows no perforation.
technique.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his infection?
o: Bacterial translocation across the gut wall
Gastric acid leaking through an ulcer

steps.x: A mechanism question about SBP.
Ascites, neutrophils >250 and E. coli with no perforation: **SBP**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: SBP arises from gut bacteria crossing the bowel wall: **bacterial translocation**.

elim: Bile peritonitis needs a biliary leak.
Acid leak means a perforated ulcer; CT shows none.
No perforation was found.
Appendicitis gives RIF pain and a secondary peritonitis.

steps.x: **A.** Rule: SBP = ascites, no perforation, translocation of gut organisms.

practice.stem: A 58 year old man has a 5 hour history of sudden severe epigastric pain which is now generalised. He takes ibuprofen daily for back pain. He is lying still. His temperature is 37.9°C, pulse rate 114 bpm and BP 112/70 mmHg. His abdomen is rigid. Chest X-ray (see item resources).
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Sudden epigastric pain on NSAIDs, a rigid abdomen and free air under the diaphragm is a perforated peptic ulcer with peritonitis. Pancreatitis does not give free air.

steps.x: Diagnosis: what has caused this peritonitis?
NSAIDs cause ulcers; sudden onset and rigidity mean perforation; the CXR shows free air.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Perforated peptic ulcer**.

elim: Cholecystitis gives RUQ pain and Murphy's sign, no free air.
Pancreatitis radiates to the back and causes no pneumoperitoneum.
MI does not give a rigid abdomen or free air.
Ruptured AAA gives back pain, shock and a pulsatile mass.

steps.x: **D.** Free air under the diaphragm = perforated viscus.

practice.stem: A 52 year old woman with alcohol-related cirrhosis has a 2 day history of fever and increasing confusion. Her abdomen is distended with shifting dullness and mild diffuse tenderness. Her temperature is 38.2°C, pulse rate 102 bpm and BP 104/62 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: A cirrhotic with ascites, fever and confusion with only mild tenderness has SBP until a tap says otherwise. A perforation would give a rigid abdomen.

steps.x: Diagnosis in a cirrhotic patient.
Ascites (shifting dullness) + fever + confusion + mild tenderness.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis**.

elim: Alcoholic hepatitis gives jaundice and tender hepatomegaly after heavy drinking.
Hepatorenal syndrome is renal failure, not fever and tenderness.
Perforation gives sudden pain and a rigid abdomen.
Portal vein thrombosis causes pain and worsening ascites, not fever.

steps.x: **E.** Cirrhosis + ascites + unwell = tap for SBP.

practice.stem: A 47 year old man has a 3 hour history of severe abdominal pain that began suddenly in the epigastrium. He has been taking prednisolone for polymyalgia. He lies still and pain worsens when he coughs. His pulse rate is 112 bpm and BP 120/76 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on abdominal examination?
practice.e: Steroids raise perforation risk; sudden pain and a still patient mean peritonitis, which gives a rigid board-like abdomen.

steps.x: A 'most likely finding' question: predict the sign of the condition.

clues: lies still and pain worsens when he coughs
steps.x: Steroids + sudden epigastric pain + still patient: perforated ulcer with **peritonitis**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Peritonitis on examination: guarding, rebound, **board-like rigidity**.

elim: Caput medusae is a sign of portal hypertension.
Murphy's sign is for cholecystitis.
A pulsatile expansile mass is an AAA.
Shifting dullness means ascites.

steps.x: **A.** Perforation = board-like abdomen.

practice.stem: A 60 year old man with cirrhosis and ascites is admitted with fever. A diagnostic paracentesis shows an ascitic neutrophil count of 410 cells/µl. Gram stain shows Gram-negative rods.
practice.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
practice.e: SBP is most often caused by E. coli, a Gram-negative gut rod, from bacterial translocation.

steps.x: An organism question for SBP.
Neutrophils >250 in ascites = SBP; Gram-negative rods narrow it further.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **E. coli**.

elim: Bacteroides is an anaerobe of secondary (perforation) peritonitis.
Candida is a fungus, not a Gram-negative rod.
S. aureus is a Gram-positive coccus.
Strep. pneumoniae is a Gram-positive coccus and less common.

steps.x: **C.** SBP = E. coli most often.

practice.stem: A 74 year old woman with known diverticular disease has a 3 day history of left iliac fossa pain and fever. Six hours ago the pain suddenly became generalised. Her temperature is 38.7°C, pulse rate 120 bpm and BP 100/64 mmHg. Her abdomen is rigid with rebound tenderness throughout.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of her peritonitis?
practice.e: Days of LIF pain and fever in known diverticular disease, then sudden generalised peritonitis, is a perforated diverticulum.

steps.x: A cause question: what has perforated?

clues: left iliac fossa pain and fever
steps.x: Diverticulitis (LIF pain, fever) that has perforated (sudden spread, generalised peritonism).

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Perforated sigmoid diverticulitis**.

elim: Mesenteric ischaemia gives pain out of proportion to signs, often with AF.
Ischaemic colitis causes bloody diarrhoea.
Volvulus gives distension and absolute constipation.
UC gives chronic bloody diarrhoea in younger patients.

steps.x: **C.** Localised LIF peritonitis + sudden generalisation = perforation.

practice.stem: A 68 year old man becomes unwell 6 hours after a colonoscopy with polypectomy. He has severe abdominal pain and distension. His pulse rate is 116 bpm and BP 106/68 mmHg. He is too unwell to sit upright, so a supine abdominal X-ray is taken.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on abdominal X-ray?
practice.e: Recent instrumentation with peritonism suggests perforation; on a supine AXR, gas outlining both sides of the bowel wall is Rigler's sign.

steps.x: A finding question: which AXR sign fits a perforation?

clues: 6 hours after a colonoscopy with polypectomy
steps.x: Instrumentation is a cause of perforation; supine film so free gas does not rise under the diaphragm.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Free gas on both sides of the bowel wall: **Rigler's sign**.

elim: Bird's beak is seen on contrast studies of volvulus or achalasia.
Coffee bean is sigmoid volvulus.
Lead-pipe colon is chronic ulcerative colitis.
Thumbprinting is bowel wall oedema in colitis or ischaemia.

steps.x: **D.** Rigler's sign = perforation on AXR.

practice.stem: A 63 year old man has a 4 hour history of sudden severe epigastric pain. He takes diclofenac. His pulse rate is 108 bpm and BP 124/80 mmHg. His abdomen is rigid with guarding. He has been given oxygen, IV fluids and analgesia, and the surgical team has been called.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
practice.e: Suspected perforation: the initial investigation is an erect chest X-ray for free air under the diaphragm, then CT for the cause.

steps.x: Initial investigation for suspected perforation.
NSAID + sudden pain + rigid abdomen: perforated ulcer suspected.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Erect chest X-ray**.

elim: Ultrasound is poor at detecting free gas.
CT colonography is an elective test for colorectal cancer.
Lipase helps diagnose pancreatitis, not perforation.
Endoscopy is avoided when perforation is suspected.

steps.x: **C.** Suspected perforation = erect CXR first.

practice.stem: A 57 year old woman with cirrhosis has worsening abdominal swelling and a temperature of 38.0°C. Her abdomen is distended with shifting dullness and is mildly tender. She is drowsier than usual.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
practice.e: Suspected SBP is diagnosed by paracentesis; an ascitic neutrophil count >250 cells/µl confirms it.

steps.x: A diagnostic investigation question in a cirrhotic.
Cirrhosis + ascites + fever + drowsiness: suspect **SBP**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Diagnostic paracentesis** with neutrophil count and culture.

elim: Ultrasound confirms ascites but not infection.
Blood cultures support but do not diagnose SBP.
CT looks for a surgical cause; it cannot diagnose SBP.
Liver biopsy assesses liver disease, not infection.

steps.x: **D.** SBP = tap the ascites; >250 neutrophils/µl.

practice.stem: A 59 year old man has generalised peritonitis. An erect chest X-ray shows free air under the diaphragm. His temperature is 38.3°C, pulse rate 118 bpm and BP 108/66 mmHg. The surgical team is on the way.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Nil by mouth, IV fluids and IV broad-spectrum antibiotics
Oral omeprazole and review in 48 hours
practice.e: Immediate management of peritonitis is NBM, IV fluids, oxygen and IV broad-spectrum antibiotics, then source control. Eradication therapy comes later.

steps.x: Initial management of peritonitis.
Perforated viscus with systemic upset: resuscitate and prepare for theatre.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **NBM, IV fluids, IV antibiotics**.

elim: Endoscopy risks enlarging a perforation.
Eradication is for later, after repair.
Oral drugs and delay are unsafe in perforation.
CT colonography is elective and irrelevant.

steps.x: **C.** Peritonitis = NBM, fluids, oxygen, IV antibiotics, then surgery.

practice.stem: A 64 year old woman has a perforated duodenal ulcer confirmed on CT. She has received IV fluids, oxygen and IV broad-spectrum antibiotics. Her pulse rate is 104 bpm and BP 116/72 mmHg. Her abdomen remains rigid.
o: Emergency surgical repair of the perforation
High-dose IV proton pump inhibitor alone
practice.e: Definitive treatment of peritonitis is to treat the cause: surgical repair of the perforation (source control). Drugs alone cannot close the hole.

steps.x: Definitive management: fix the source.

clues: perforated duodenal ulcer confirmed on CT
steps.x: Ongoing peritonitis from a known perforation.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Surgical repair** (e.g. omental patch) and washout.

elim: A PPI helps healing but does not seal a free perforation.
Embolisation treats bleeding, not perforation.
Antibiotics without source control fail.
Endoscopy is not used for free perforation.

steps.x: **A.** Peritonitis = source control.
